summary: 37 units reviewed (75-111). 3 error, 28 minor issues; 3 errors: unit 79 English adds 'number' to a doubtful reading, unit 107 Hindi translates part of a damaged word and uses मधुमेह (the modern diabetes name). The drafter's text flags are sound: real or very likely misprints in 84 (chandrabindu '~', an artifact), 91, 93 (15 syllables, cūrṇayitvā), 98 (kathite for kvathite), 100 (stray r), 105, 107 (14 syllables), 110 (śiśirānte); speculative in 76 (the 'vi' insertion), 79 (saptarātrāt invented) and 99 (maireyān a guess). Printed form is kept in words for 79, 99, 107 (good); words for 76 rely on a reconstruction. Unit 107 left untranslated: correct, no safe reading exists. kaṣāya is the decoction sense everywhere in this chunk, no taste sense. No effects are stated that the text does not state (104 and 103 translate statements actually in the Sanskrit). Cross-unit sentences: 75-76 (locatives + yojyaḥ), 88-89, 102-103, 105-108 are handled but 89 and 106-107 notes need a cross-reference (patches given). Regrouping: no change of unit boundaries; but the 'forms one verse with unit N' claims in every unit rest on an unproven pairing (see glossary_suggestions); syntactic groups are 75-76, 88-89, 102-103, 105-106 (negative) then 107-108 (positive), then 109-110.

glossary_suggestions.suggestion: English: madhumeha ('honey-urine'). Hindi: the usual word मधुमेह now means diabetes; choose one non-modern form for the whole book (for example the hyphenated मधु-मेह, as यक्ष्मन् was chosen over यक्ष्मा) and apply it everywhere. Same check for पाण्डु, गुल्म, उदावर्त.

Keep 'decoction' for the preparation sense (all uses in this chunk, units 83, 89-90, 94-95, 101-102, are the preparation); write 'astringent taste (kaṣāya)' only where the taste is meant. 'hima' + kaṣāya is rendered 'cold decoction'.

Fix wording without a supplied pronoun: pāyayet = 'should cause to drink' (no '(him)'), nidhāpayet = 'should cause to be placed' or 'should place' (choose one), bhāvayet = 'should saturate'. The parenthetical '(him)' used in units 83 and 91 adds a gender.
Keep 'maṇḍa' with one fixed short gloss (e.g. 'upper part, scum'); do not define it as 'clear'.
Medical-term rule says no plant identification: either keep 'yava' in all languages or record 'yava = barley' once as an accepted plain grain word.

Do not write 'forms one verse with unit N' as a fact: the printed lines all end in a double danda and the syntax gives mixed evidence (75-76, 71-72, 73-74 pair as odd+even; 80-81, 86-87, 88-89 read better as even+odd). Use 'GROUPING:' only for clear sentence links.
